title: OpenAI says its coding agents now finish 46% of 2–4 hour research tasks, up from 23% in March
subtitle: The 'jagged frontier' report shows agents strong on monitoring work, weak on building evaluations and RL setups — and the task mix itself keeps shifting.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI published its 'Research Acceleration: The Jagged Frontier' report on November 18, 2026. The headline figure: its coding agents now complete, without human help, about 46% of research tasks that take a human researcher two to four hours. That is up from 23% in March 2026. For longer tasks of four to eight hours, success rose from 13% to 35%. The capability is uneven. Agents succeed on roughly 79% of tasks that involve monitoring training runs, but only about 29% of work that involves building evaluations, reinforcement learning setups and agent environments. The figures reflect how OpenAI's own researchers used the tools in October.

The 'jagged frontier' framing is the honest part. The improvement is real, but it is not uniform, and the benefit depends on whether a researcher's work maps onto the strengths. Monitoring is routine, pattern-recognition heavy, and rewarding to automate; building an eval suite requires judgment about what to measure and why, and remains a human job. The report also notes that researchers shifted which tasks they delegated to agents as the agents improved. That changes the comparison between March and October: part of the lift is better agents, part is better task selection by humans.

This is a company self-report, not an independent benchmark, and no other lab can reproduce the numbers without matching the task definitions and researcher population. That is a meaningful caveat. But it is also the most honest snapshot anybody has published about how frontier AI agents actually perform inside the labs building them. Anthropic's R&D Automation Index, released in September, claimed Claude 'leads at 26%' on a similar-shaped internal measurement — the two are not directly comparable, but the shape of the curve is consistent across labs. The frontier of autonomous research work is somewhere between 25% and 50% of mid-length tasks, depending on who is counting.

A note for learners: the gap between monitoring (79%) and building (29%) is the most portable finding in the report. If you are an early-career engineer or researcher deciding where to spend your time, the work that still rewards human judgment is the work of defining problems, designing evaluations, and choosing what to measure. The work of running the measurements and watching the dials is increasingly agent-automatable. Build in the direction the curve is bending toward — not the direction it is bending away from.
